column1: # roog's compatibility matrix: one row per machine roog claims to run on.
# This file is the pipeline. `cross_build.sh` builds a row, `stress_test_matrix.sh`
# runs a row under emulation with the row's limits applied, and the report prints
# a row per row. Adding a machine is adding a line here; nothing else knows the
# list. (Same rule as the content tables -- see docs/explanation/adr-0001-tables-not-raws.md.)
# Columns, tab-separated:
#   id        short name, used for file names and report rows
#   target    rust target triple
#   class     linux  -- has an OS, a terminal and a shell; roog runs here
#             bare   -- no OS; only `particle-core` is built, and only checked
#   platform  docker --platform value for a `native` row, or "-" for bare
#             metal. A `qemu` row's container runs as the host's own
#             architecture instead (see stress_test_matrix.sh), so this
#             column only tells it which static interpreter to fetch.
#   image     runtime image the binary is executed in, or the SDK image for bare
#   exec      native -- the host CPU runs it directly
#             qemu   -- run under a directly-invoked qemu-user-static
#                        interpreter; needs no binfmt_misc and no --privileged
#             none   -- not executed at all (bare metal)
#   cpus      docker --cpus, the CPU budget that stands in for the hardware
#   memory    docker --memory, the RAM the machine actually has
#   note      what real machine this row is standing in for
# The limits are deliberately mean. A container that can use four modern cores
# tells you nothing about a Pi; the point of a row is to be as slow as the thing
# it names, not to pass.
